nodes.statement: Clause 1: prove or refute that each r≥1 has infinitely many class-r primes under the exact class predicate.

Clause 2: determine the actual bounded/divergent/limit or sharper behavior of p_r^(1/r) on every r for which p_r is defined; if clause 1 is negative, separately handle existence of p_r in the range needed for the asymptotic clause.
Both clauses use one consistent class definition.

For the growth/classification clause, give a complete asymptotic classification sufficient to distinguish the stated alternatives; one-sided unboundedness, limsup-only, or liminf-only information is not by itself a complete classification.
COMPLETE TWO-CLAUSE DETERMINATION: determine infinitude in every class and give a mathematically decisive asymptotic classification of p_r^(1/r).
A single prime in a class proves only nonemptiness, not infinitude; infinitude of class 1 does not imply infinitude of all classes.
Any negative/mixed result uses the same exact IsOfClass predicate and class index in every clause.
COMPLETE NEGATIVE/MIXED DETERMINATION: any negative answer uses the exact quantifier negation, and the p_r^(1/r) behavior is still fully classified.

A prime $p$ is in class $1$ if the only prime divisors of $p+1$ are $2$ or $3$. In general, a prime $p$ is in class $r$ if every prime factor of $p+1$ is in some class $\leq r-1$, with equality for at least one prime factor.Are there infinitely many primes in each class? If $p_r$ is the least prime in class $r$, then how does $p_r^{1/r}$ behave?
